questions.q: Why does the characteristic function φ(t) = E[e^{itX}] always exist, while the moment-generating function M(t) = E[e^{tX}] sometimes does not?
options: Because φ(t) is only defined for discrete random variables
Because |e^{itX}| = 1 for every real t, keeping the expectation bounded, while e^{tX} can grow without bound
Because the characteristic function ignores the tails of the distribution
Because M(t) is only defined for normal distributions
questions.explain: Since |e^{itX}| = 1 always, E[e^{itX}] is bounded by 1 in magnitude and always exists. e^{tX}, by contrast, can grow arbitrarily large for heavy-tailed distributions, so its expectation can diverge.

questions.q: If M(t) is the MGF of X, what does M''(0), the second derivative evaluated at t = 0, equal?
questions.explain: Differentiating M(t) = E[e^{tX}] twice and evaluating at 0 gives M''(0) = E[X²], the second raw moment. Variance would require subtracting (E[X])² afterward.

questions.q: X and Y are independent random variables. What is the moment-generating function of X + Y?
options: The convolution of M_X and M_Y
questions.explain: Independence lets E[e^{t(X+Y)}] = E[e^{tX}]E[e^{tY}] split the expectation of a product into a product of expectations, so M_{X+Y}(t) = M_X(t)·M_Y(t).

questions.q: For X ~ N(μ, σ²), the MGF is M(t) = exp(μt + ½σ²t²). What is M'(0)?
questions.explain: M'(t) = (μ + σ²t)·M(t), so M'(0) = (μ + 0)·1 = μ, confirming E[X] = μ for the normal distribution.

questions.q: Why are characteristic functions especially useful in derivatives pricing models like Heston's stochastic volatility model?
options: Because the characteristic function is always exactly 1
Because the model's characteristic function is known in closed form even when its probability density is not, enabling Fourier-based pricing methods like Carr-Madan
Because characteristic functions eliminate the need for any numerical computation
Because they only apply to European call options
questions.explain: Several important pricing models have characteristic functions available in closed form but no simple closed-form density. Methods like Carr-Madan exploit this by pricing options directly via the characteristic function using the FFT.
